questions.q: Why is the normalization condition |a|²+|b|²=1 physically required, rather than just a mathematical convention?
options: Because |a|² and |b|² are the measurement probabilities of outcomes 0 and 1, and since those are the only two possible outcomes, their probabilities must sum to exactly 1
Because quantum hardware would be damaged by an unnormalized state
Because |0⟩ and |1⟩ are themselves not normalized unless the full state is
There is no real physical requirement -- it is purely a notational convention chosen for convenience
questions.explain: Normalization follows directly from the Born rule: since P(0)=|a|² and P(1)=|b|² are the only two possible outcomes, they must sum to 1, exactly as any valid probability distribution must.

questions.q: For |ψ⟩=√(1/3)|0⟩+√(2/3)|1⟩, what are P(0) and P(1), and is this state normalized?
options: P(0)=1/3≈0.333, P(1)=2/3≈0.667, and yes it's normalized since 1/3+2/3=1
P(0)=√(1/3), P(1)=√(2/3), and it is not normalized
P(0)=P(1)=0.5 regardless of the stated amplitudes
This state cannot be normalized because the amplitudes are irrational
questions.explain: Squaring each amplitude gives P(0)=(√(1/3))²=1/3 and P(1)=(√(2/3))²=2/3 (verified), and 1/3+2/3=1 confirms normalization. Irrational amplitudes are perfectly fine -- normalization only constrains the sum of squared magnitudes.

questions.q: What is a 'global phase,' and why is it physically unobservable?
options: A factor e^(iθ) multiplying the ENTIRE state vector; it cancels out of every measurement probability in every basis, so two states differing only by it are physically identical
A phase that only appears on the |1⟩ amplitude, never on |0⟩
A type of normalization error that makes a state invalid
A phase that changes measurement probabilities but not the state's energy
questions.explain: Global phase multiplies the whole vector equally, so it factors out of every |amplitude|² calculation and every inner product's magnitude -- nothing observable depends on it, unlike a relative phase between individual amplitudes.

questions.q: Why does changing 0.6|0⟩+0.8|1⟩ to 0.6|0⟩+0.9|1⟩ count as a genuine error, while changing |0⟩ to −|0⟩ does not?
options: 0.6²+0.9²=1.17≠1 breaks normalization and describes no valid state, while −|0⟩ is just |0⟩ multiplied by a global phase (e^(iπ)), which is physically identical to |0⟩
Both changes are equally invalid because any change to a state's written amplitudes is an error
Both changes are equally valid because normalization only applies to positive amplitudes
0.6|0⟩+0.9|1⟩ is valid because 0.6+0.9 is close to 1
questions.explain: The first change violates the normalization condition and so describes no real quantum state; the second is a global phase applied to the whole vector, which changes nothing measurable, so it's just a different valid way to write the same physical state.

questions.q: Why does global-phase invariance matter in practice when comparing outputs from two different quantum simulators or algorithms?
options: Two mathematically different-looking state vectors can both be correct if they differ only by an overall phase, so naive vector equality can give a false mismatch
It means simulators never need to normalize their output vectors
It means any two state vectors are always physically equivalent, regardless of their amplitudes
It only matters for multi-qubit states, never for single qubits
questions.explain: Because an overall phase factor is unobservable, two correct simulators can return vectors that differ by exactly such a factor and still both be right -- comparing raw amplitudes for exact equality without accounting for this can incorrectly flag a correct result as wrong.
